lesson_title: Molar Gas Volume: Same Crate, Any Cargo
hook_text: 44 grams of CO2. 2 grams of hydrogen. Exactly the same box. Every time.
clip_script: Take one mole of carbon dioxide — 44 grams. Take one mole of hydrogen — a feathery 2 grams. Same temperature, same pressure: they fill exactly the same volume. How? A gas is almost entirely empty space — a dozen flies in a school hall. The volume is set by the spacing between molecules, and temperature and pressure decide that spacing, not the cargo's mass. At STP the shared crate has a number: 22,4 cubic decimetres for every mole of any gas. So 13 grams of zinc fizzing in acid — a fifth of a mole of hydrogen — fills a fifth of a crate: 4,48 litres. More than two cooldrink bottles of gas, from one spoonful of grey metal.
visual_style: Two identical wireframe crates side by side; a featherweight molecule and a heavyweight molecule drop in and the crates stay the same size; a spoon of zinc granules erupts into bottles filling with gas.
pacing: Provocative mismatch up front, quick empty-space explainer, fizzing bottle payoff.
